### AIM-58 — Registration requires no verified email or phone, no captcha, and issues full tokens immediately

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/api/validators/auth.validator.ts:34`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/services/auth.service.ts:45`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/config/env.ts:89`
**Checklist:** P5.1 signup abuse - mass account creation, verification enforced before the account can act, captcha or rate limit — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
export const registerSchema = z.object({
  account: accountSchema,
  password: passwordSchema,
  fcmTokens: fcmTokensSchema.optional().default([]),
});
```

**Impact.** `register` (auth.service.ts:28) creates the user and immediately calls `issueAuthTokens`, so the account is fully usable - it can send friend requests, create communities, mint presigned upload URLs and message anyone who accepts. There is no email/phone field to verify, no captcha anywhere in either repo, and the only brake is `sensitiveAuthRateLimiter` at 20 per 15 minutes per IP (SENSITIVE_AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX default 20). That is ~1,900 accounts/day from a single address and unbounded from a botnet, and it is the multiplier behind every other abuse item here (friend-request spam, community add-spam, storage fill).

**Fix.** Require a verified email or phone before the account leaves a restricted state (media upload, community creation and outbound friend requests gated on it), and add a proof-of-work or captcha challenge on POST /auth/register.

### AIM-59 — Offset pagination accepts an unbounded page number on every paged endpoint

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/user-service/src/api/validators/user-search.validator.ts:27`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/user-service/src/api/validators/friendship.validator.ts:32`, `aimess_backend/apps/user-service/src/api/validators/user-discovery.validator.ts:6`, `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/api/validators/community.validator.ts:46`
**Checklist:** P5.5 pagination/query DoS - unbounded limit/pageSize accepted from the client — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
page: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(1),
```

**Impact.** `limit` is capped everywhere (max 10-200), but `page` has no upper bound in any validator, and it is multiplied into Prisma's `skip` (user-profile.repository.ts:216/247, friendship.repository.ts:562). `?page=100000000` makes the database walk and discard a hundred million rows per request; the same call also issues an unbounded `count()` over a LIKE filter. Neither user-service nor community-service mounts any rate limiter of its own, and the gateway's `searchRateLimiter` / `readRateLimiter` are never mounted (see separate finding), so these land under the 100-per-15-minutes global backstop only.

**Fix.** Cap `page` (e.g. `.max(1000)`) in the shared page schemas, or reject `skip` beyond a fixed ceiling in the repositories and require cursor pagination past it.

### AIM-60 — Community invite links never expire and default to unlimited uses

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/services/community.service.ts:1481`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/services/community.service.ts:9694`
**Checklist:** P5.4 invite abuse - unlimited redemption, no expiry, no max-uses — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
if (link.maxUses !== null && link.usedCount >= link.maxUses)
    throw new GoneError("COMMUNITY_INVITE_LINK_EXHAUSTED");
```

**Impact.** `assertInviteLinkActive` checks only `revokedAt` and `maxUses`; `createInviteLink` writes `expiresAt: null` unconditionally (line 9694) and the surrounding comments confirm nothing stamps or reads an expiry. A bare create call defaults `maxUses` to null, i.e. unlimited redemptions. Any ACTIVE member (not just a moderator) can mint links, and the per-member cap on simultaneously-active links was removed. A private community's link, once leaked or posted publicly, grants join access forever to an unbounded number of people until an admin notices and revokes it by hand; there is no audit trigger for anomalous redemption volume.

**Fix.** Stamp and enforce an `expiresAt` (default 7 or 30 days) in `createInviteLink` and check it in `assertInviteLinkActive`; default `maxUses` to a finite number for non-moderator creators.

### AIM-61 — Livestream creation is unthrottled and PENDING streams are exempt from the concurrency caps

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/stream-service/src/services/livestream.service.ts:374`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/stream-service/src/api/routes/index.ts:14`
**Checklist:** P5.2 broadcast amplification; P5.8 notification bombing — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
const [activeAnywhere, activeByCommunity] = await Promise.all([
          this.streamRepo.countLiveByCreator(params.creatorId),
          this.streamRepo.countActiveByCommunity(params.communityId),
        ]);
```

**Impact.** The comment two lines above states the counts are "all LIVE-only (PENDING never blocks)", and `create` inserts with `status: "PENDING"`. stream-service mounts no rate limiter anywhere (POST /streams carries only `authenticateAccessToken`, api/routes/index.ts:14). A community moderator can therefore loop POST /streams: each call mints a 16-byte stream key, writes a row, and publishes a `stream.created` event that fans out to the whole community - unbounded DB rows and unbounded community-wide notifications, none of which trip the LIVE concurrency guard.

**Fix.** Count PENDING rows toward the per-creator cap (or expire PENDING rows after a short TTL), and add a per-user Redis create limiter in front of `createStream`.

### AIM-62 — Redis-backed rate limiters across three services fail open on any cache error

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/middleware/rate-limit.ts:176`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/lib/invite-rate-limit.ts:30`, `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/lib/otp-rate-limit.ts:34`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/stream.ns.ts:578`
**Checklist:** P5.2 messaging spam; P5.4 invite abuse; P5.8 OTP abuse — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
} catch (err) {
      // If Redis is unavailable, allow the request through
      logFailOpen(keyPrefix, "redis_error", err);
      next();
    }
```

**Impact.** Every abuse counter that is not express-rate-limit fails open by design: chat-service's message limiters here, community-service's invite create/bulk caps (invite-rate-limit.ts:30 returns early when the cache is not ready), auth-service's OTP issuance throttle (otp-rate-limit.ts:34), and the livestream comment limiter (stream.ns.ts:578). A Redis outage - or any deployment where the community cache is simply disabled - silently removes all of them at once, at exactly the moment the platform is least able to absorb a flood. The fail-open is logged but nothing gates on it.

**Fix.** Keep fail-open for read paths, but fail closed (or degrade to a strict in-process fallback counter) for the send/OTP/invite write paths, and alert on the `rate_limit_fail_open` log line so an outage is not silent.

### AIM-63 — Per-socket presence maps grow without bound from attacker-supplied conversation ids

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/presence-indicator.ts:105`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/chat.ns.ts:1857`
**Checklist:** P5.6 socket abuse - typing-event flood, unbounded per-connection state — flagged by P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
timers.set(
        roomId,
        setTimeout(() => {
          timers.delete(roomId);
          emit(roomId, stopEvent, true);
        }, ttlMs)
      );
```

**Impact.** `start()` writes into the `timers` map and arms a setTimeout before `broadcast` runs its authorization, and `rememberTypingHint` (chat.ns.ts:1857) writes into `typingHints` before any check at all. `conversationId` is any string with min length 1. Emitting typing:start with a fresh random id each time allocates one map entry plus one live timer per event on the gateway process; entries only drain after the 6s TTL, so a sustained loop keeps hundreds of thousands of timers and strings resident. Same shape for `recordingNames`.

**Fix.** Authorize before allocating: resolve the roster (or at minimum check the socket is in `conv:<id>`) before writing to `typingHints`/`recordingNames`/`timers`, and cap the number of distinct rooms a socket may hold presence state for.

### AIM-64 — Password-reset request is a user-enumeration oracle (contradicting its own comment and the admin equivalent)

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/services/password-reset.service.ts:64`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/services/password-reset.service.ts:65`
**Checklist:** P4.3 password reset — no user-enumeration difference between "email not found" and "email sent" — flagged by P4/P5 Authentication, P5 Feature abuse & limits

```
if (!user || !canResetPassword(user)) {
      throw new NotFoundError("AUTH_PASSWORD_RESET_EMAIL_NOT_FOUND");
    }
```

**Impact.** POST /api/v1/auth/forgot-password/request answers 404 AUTH_PASSWORD_RESET_EMAIL_NOT_FOUND for an unknown address and 200 for a registered one, so an attacker can confirm membership for any email address by status code alone. The comment at line 176-177 of the same file asserts requestOtp "deliberately keeps its ambiguous 'if this email is registered' answer" — it does not. The backoffice twin gets this right (apps/backoffice-service/src/services/admin-password-reset.service.ts:61-64 returns silently). The gateway limiter is IP-scoped (10/15min) and, as noted separately, the auth-service one is X-Forwarded-For-spoofable, so bulk enumeration is practical.

**Fix.** Return 200 with the same neutral body whether or not the address resolves — move the OTP issuance inside the `if (user && canResetPassword(user))` branch and drop the throw, exactly as adminPasswordResetService.requestOtp does.

### AIM-65 — Access tokens carry no issuer or audience claim and are verified with a secret shared by eight services

**Where:** `aimess_backend/packages/auth-jwt/src/access-token.ts:43`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/packages/auth-jwt/src/access-token.ts:64`, `aimess_backend/packages/auth-jwt/src/access-token.ts:115`
**Checklist:** P4.1 JWT — audience/issuer validation — flagged by P4/P5 Authentication

```
return jwt.sign(payload, params.secret, {
    expiresIn: params.expiresInSeconds,
  });
```

**Impact.** signAccessToken sets no `iss` and no `aud`, and verifyAccessToken (line 64-66) validates only the algorithm and the `type`/`sub`/`sid` shape. The same JWT_ACCESS_SECRET is deployed to api-gateway, auth-service, user-service, chat-service, community-service, stream-service, media-service and notifications-service (each service's config/env.ts requires it). Any one of those eight environments being read — a leaked container env, a debug endpoint, an SSRF into a metadata service — lets the reader forge a token for any userId with role "ADMIN", accepted platform-wide with no way to scope or attribute it. There is also no `kid`, so rotating the secret invalidates every live session at once rather than allowing overlap.

**Fix.** Add `issuer: "aimess-auth"` and an `audience` on sign, and assert both in verifyAccessToken/verifyAdminAccessToken. Longer term, move to an asymmetric key (RS256/EdDSA) so only auth-service holds the private key and the other seven services hold a public key that cannot mint tokens.

### AIM-66 — POST /auth/token mints access tokens from a refresh token without rotating it, so a stolen refresh token never trips reuse detection

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/services/session.service.ts:166`
**Checklist:** P4.2 logout/revocation — refresh-token rotation, replay of a stolen refresh token — flagged by P4/P5 Authentication

```
async issueAccessToken(refreshToken: string): Promise<AccessTokenResponse> {
    const tokenHash = hashToken(refreshToken);
    const stored = await refreshTokenRepository.findByTokenHash(tokenHash);
```

**Impact.** refresh() (line 140) rotates the refresh token and is what arms the `rotatedToId` tripwire that revokes every session on reuse. issueAccessToken performs the identical validation but returns only an access token and never calls rotate(), so the refresh token stays valid and unmarked. An attacker who exfiltrates a refresh token (it sits in localStorage, see the separate finding) can poll /api/v1/auth/token indefinitely for fresh 1-hour access tokens and will never trigger the reuse alarm, because the tripwire only fires when a token that HAS been rotated is presented again. Neither endpoint is rate-limited at the gateway (routes/v1/index.ts:74-93 lists neither) beyond the 100/min global backstop.

**Fix.** Either rotate on this path too (call refreshTokenRepository.rotate and return the new refresh token), or record a per-refresh-token use counter/last-used timestamp and revoke on anomalous use. At minimum add /auth/refresh and /auth/token to the gateway's sensitive-path limiter list.

### AIM-67 — Password policy is length-only: 8 characters, no complexity, no breach or reuse check

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/api/validators/auth.validator.ts:20`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/backoffice-service/src/config/env.ts:80`
**Checklist:** P4.4 login — credential strength / brute-force resistance — flagged by P4/P5 Authentication

```
export const passwordSchema = z
    .string()
    .min(8, "Password must be at least 8 characters")
    .max(128, "Password must be at most 128 characters");
```

**Impact.** This schema governs registration, password reset completion and change-password. "password", "12345678" and "aimess12" all pass. Combined with the auth-service rate limiter being X-Forwarded-For-spoofable (separate finding), the practical brake on credential stuffing is the 5-attempt per-account lockout, which a low-and-slow spray across many accounts sidesteps. Admin accounts are worse: BOOTSTRAP_SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD is `z.string().min(6)` (backoffice config/env.ts:80).

**Fix.** Raise the minimum to 12, reject the top-N common-password list (a static set is enough — no new dependency needed), and raise BOOTSTRAP_SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD to min(16).

### AIM-68 — Debug logging decodes the unverified JWT payload and logs req.auth on every community-service request

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/middleware/authenticate-access-token.ts:29`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/middleware/require-platform-admin.ts:13`

```
function decodeUnverifiedForDebug(header: string | undefined) {

```

**Impact.** Marked "TEMPORARY DEBUG — remove once the /categories/admin 401 investigation is closed" but still shipped. It base64-decodes the token payload without verification and logs type/role/sub-presence for every request (line 59-64), and logs the full resolved `req.auth` afterwards (line 71). The claims logged are attacker-controlled before verification, so log output on an unauthenticated request reflects whatever an attacker puts in an unsigned token — log injection into whatever aggregator ingests these, plus per-request userId/sessionId written to disk. requirePlatformAdmin carries the same leftover debug logger (require-platform-admin.ts:13). The decode result is never used for an authorization decision, so this is hygiene rather than a bypass.

### AIM-69 — Attachment guard passes any http(s) value through, and the read path returns it verbatim as the media URL

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/lib/attachment-guard.ts:54`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/lib/media-resolve.ts:53`, `aimess_backend/apps/media-service/src/services/media.service.ts:528`
**Checklist:** P4/P5.3 trusting client-supplied values — an attacker-chosen URL is accepted as a media reference and served to other users — flagged by P4/P5 Authorization & IDOR

```
for (const candidate of [file.objectKey, file.thumbnailObjectKey, file.url]) {
    if (typeof candidate !== "string" || candidate.length === 0) continue;
    if (isHttpUrl(candidate)) continue; // external provider — not our object
```

**Impact.** `assertAttachmentsVerified` deliberately skips any candidate matching /^https?:\/\//i, and there is no allowlist of provider hosts (the doc comment names Giphy/Tenor as the intent). On read, `resolveMediaUrl` returns the same value unchanged (lib/media-resolve.ts:53 `if (isHttpUrl(stored)) return stored;`), and media-service's own download-url endpoint short-circuits identically (apps/media-service/src/services/media.service.ts:528-545). So any sender can post a message whose attachment `objectKey` is `https://attacker.example/beacon.png`, and every recipient's client fetches attacker-controlled content the moment the message renders: no magic-byte validation, no AV scan, no size cap, and the attacker's host learns each recipient's IP, User-Agent and read timing. The same field also reaches push payloads via `pushImageKeyOf` (lib/media-resolve.ts:119-125).

**Fix.** Replace the blanket `isHttpUrl` bypass with an explicit host allowlist (media.giphy.com, tenor.com, ... ) checked against the parsed URL's hostname, and reject everything else with the same `MEDIA_NOT_VERIFIED` error the object path uses. Apply it in `storageKeysOf` so the guard covers `objectKey`, `thumbnailObjectKey` and `url`, and mirror it in media-service's `generateDownloadUrl` short-circuit so both surfaces agree.

### AIM-70 — Attachment ownership/scope/scan gate is disabled wholesale by a runtime flag with no production guard

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/lib/attachment-guard.ts:77`
**Checklist:** P4/P5.2 IDOR — the media ownership/scope check that prevents attaching another user's object is defeatable by configuration — flagged by P4/P5 Authorization & IDOR


**Impact.** A single env var turns off all three checks the guard performs — scan-verified, registry ownerId == sender, registry resourceId == this room — for every send path in the service (private, group and community). With it false, a user attaches any object key they can name to any room, and because chat-service presigns MinIO directly on read (lib/media-resolve.ts:57) media-service's authz never runs either, so the object becomes readable by that room's whole audience. The default is `true` (config/env.ts:85-88) and .env.example sets it, but nothing prevents the value being false in production. Compare `withServiceAuth` (packages/grpc-utils/src/index.ts:126-130), which throws at boot when its secret is missing in production — that is the pattern this switch is missing.

**Fix.** Refuse to start when `NODE_ENV === "production"` and `CHAT_MEDIA_VERIFY_ENABLED` is false, mirroring the gRPC service-token boot check; keep the escape hatch for non-production only.

### AIM-71 — Request body size is unbounded on every proxied route — the body parsers are mounted AFTER the /admin and /api proxies

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/app.ts:96`
**Checklist:** P3.4 body size limits / request timeout — flagged by P3 Edge controls

```
app.use("/admin", createAdminRouter());
  app.use("/api", createApiRouter(messagingClient));

  app.use(express.json({ limit: "1mb" }));
  app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true, limit: "1mb" }));
```

**Impact.** http-proxy-middleware streams the raw request body upstream, and Express middleware only runs on routes reached before the handler that answers. Because `express.json({limit:'1mb'})` sits at line 96 — after the /admin mount (91) and the /api mount (94) — no size limit is ever applied at the gateway to any proxied request; those parsers only ever see requests that fall through to the 404 handler. The production HAProxy edge (deploy/haproxy/dev02.cfg) sets no body-size cap either — the 2m `client_max_body_size` lives only in deploy/nginx/sites/dev02-api.conf:40, whose own header marks it SUPERSEDED BY HAPROXY. An unauthenticated caller can POST a multi-gigabyte body to /api/v1/auth/login and hold gateway plus upstream sockets and memory until the downstream 1mb parser finally aborts, one connection per request.

**Fix.** Add an explicit size guard before the proxy mounts — a Content-Length/stream-length check middleware in front of `app.use("/admin")` — or restore a body-size cap at the HAProxy frontend in deploy/haproxy/dev02.cfg. Leaving the 1mb parsers where they are is harmless but does nothing.

### AIM-72 — Gateway rate limiters use an in-process memory store that resets on restart and is not shared across replicas

**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/middleware/rate-limit.ts:128`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/middleware/rate-limit.ts:190`, `aimess_backend/deploy/nginx/sites/dev02-api.conf:19`
**Checklist:** P5.3 gateway edge controls — flagged by P3 Edge controls, P5 Feature abuse & limits, P5 Internal exposure

```

 * one counter per Node process, not shared across replicas, wiped on restart.
```

**Impact.** The credential-stuffing and OTP limiters (sensitiveAuthRateLimiter at line 190, otpRateLimiter) hold their counters in process memory. Today deploy/dev02/compose.yml runs a single api-gateway container so the practical impact is limited to counters being wiped by any restart or redeploy - an attacker who can trigger or simply wait for a deploy resets their budget. The moment a second gateway replica is added (deploy/nginx/sites/dev02-api.conf:19 already carries ip_hash 'before a second gateway pod is added'), every limit multiplies by the replica count and ip_hash lets a client pick its own replica by source address. **Fix.** Swap in rate-limit-redis against the existing REDIS_URL, and set passOnStoreError: true as the comment at line 131 already notes, so a Redis blip fails open rather than 500ing every request. Do this before adding a second gateway replica.

### AIM-80 — SMTP transport does not require TLS on non-465 ports, so OTP emails can be relayed in cleartext

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/notifications-service/src/providers/mail/transporter.ts:7`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/backoffice-service/src/lib/admin-mailer.ts:9`
**Checklist:** P2.3 third-party sends (email/SMS providers) — flagged by P2 Personal-data flow

```
export const transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({ host: env.SMTP_HOST, port: env.SMTP_PORT, secure: env.SMTP_PORT === 465, auth: { user: env.SMTP_USER, pass: env.SMTP_PASS } });
```

**Impact.** With any port other than 465 (587 is the common production choice) `secure` is false and nodemailer only OPPORTUNISTICALLY upgrades via STARTTLS - `requireTLS` is not set, so if the relay does not advertise STARTTLS, or an on-path attacker strips the capability from the EHLO response, nodemailer silently continues in cleartext and sends the SMTP AUTH credentials plus the message body. The bodies here are registration, password-reset, link-email and change-email OTP codes (providers/mail/templates/*), so a downgrade hands an on-path observer a live account-recovery code together with the recipient address.

**Fix.** Add `requireTLS: true` (and ideally `tls: { minVersion: "TLSv1.2" }`) to both transports so a relay without STARTTLS fails the send instead of falling back to plaintext.


**Impact.** Every keystroke in the composer writes the in-progress message body to localStorage under `aimess:draft:<threadId>`. Logout (useAuth.ts:113-123) clears Redux, the TanStack cache and IndexedDB via clearOfflineDatabase(), and draftsSlice zeroes its own mirror on logoutSuccess (draftsSlice.ts:34) - but nothing removes the `aimess:draft:*` localStorage keys. On a shared or kiosk browser the next person to sign in still has the previous user's unsent message text sitting in localStorage, readable from devtools and from any script on the origin. `aimess.threadAlias` (threadAlias.ts:6) and the wallpaper data-URL library (wallpaper-client.ts:56) persist across logout the same way.

**Fix.** In the logout path, iterate Object.keys(localStorage) and remove anything matching /^aimess:draft:/ alongside the existing clearOfflineDatabase() call, and drop `aimess.threadAlias` there too.

### AIM-82 — Static long-lived TURN credentials shipped in the public client bundle

**Where:** `aimess_website/src/configs/app.config.ts:54`
**Also at:** `aimess_website/src/utils/srs.ts:96`
**Checklist:** P2.3 third-party sends / outbound credential exposure — flagged by P2 Personal-data flow

```
turnUsername: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_TURN_USERNAME || "", turnCredential: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_TURN_CREDENTIAL || "",
```

**Impact.** Both are NEXT_PUBLIC_*, so the TURN username and shared secret are inlined verbatim into the JS bundle and handed to every visitor, authenticated or not, via buildIceServers() (srs.ts:96-97). They are static - there is no time-limited REST-credential mechanism anywhere in the codebase - so anyone who views source gets a permanent relay credential and can use the TURN server as a free anonymous proxy, attributing that traffic to AIMESS's infrastructure and consuming its bandwidth quota.

**Fix.** Issue ephemeral TURN credentials server-side: add an authenticated endpoint on the gateway that returns a `username = <expiry>:<userId>` / `credential = base64(HMAC-SHA1(secret, username))` pair with a short TTL (the standard coturn REST API), keep the shared secret server-only, and have srs.ts fetch the ICE server list instead of reading it from appConfig.

### AIM-83 — api-gateway defaults NODE_ENV to "development", which turns off CORS origin enforcement at the only public edge

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/config/env.ts:15`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/config/env.ts:196`, `aimess_backend/apps/media-service/src/config/env.ts:10`
**Checklist:** P3.2 NODE_ENV check that defaults to development behaviour in production — flagged by P3 Pre-deploy audit

```
NODE_ENV: z
    .enum(["development", "production", "test"])
    .default("development"),
...
export function isCorsOriginAllowed(origin: string | undefined): boolean {
  if (!origin) return true;
  if (env.NODE_ENV === "development") return true;   // line 196
```

**Impact.** Seven of the nine services declare NODE_ENV as a required z.enum with no default and refuse to boot without it; api-gateway and media-service instead default it to "development". The gateway is the single public entry point, and its CORS validator returns true for every origin when NODE_ENV is "development" (line 196), which is also the validator the Socket.IO server uses. An unset, misspelled, or dropped NODE_ENV in the compose env_file therefore silently converts the production edge into an allow-any-origin edge - `credentials: true` is set on the same options object (apps/api-gateway/src/app.ts:34), so any attacker-controlled page can then make credentialed cross-origin calls to the whole API. The failure is completely silent: nothing logs the fallback.

**Fix.** Make NODE_ENV a required z.enum with no default in api-gateway and media-service, matching the other seven services, and invert isCorsOriginAllowed to enforce the allowlist unless NODE_ENV is explicitly "development".

### AIM-84 — JWT signing secrets are validated as bare z.string() in three services - an empty or one-character secret passes boot validation

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/config/env.ts:20`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/auth-service/src/config/env.ts:21`, `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/config/env.ts:34`, `aimess_backend/apps/notifications-service/src/config/env.ts:65`
**Checklist:** P3.1 env validation - critical secrets not properly validated — flagged by P3 Pre-deploy audit, P4/P5 Authentication

```
JWT_ACCESS_SECRET: z.string(),
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET: z.string(),
```

**Impact.** api-gateway, user-service, community-service, stream-service and media-service all declare JWT_ACCESS_SECRET as z.string().min(1); auth-service (the issuer, for both the access and the refresh secret), chat-service (line 34) and notifications-service (line 65) declare it with no constraint at all. A truncated deploy variable, a bad shell quote, or an operator picking a short value yields a secret like "" or "x" that passes validation and boots the whole platform. A single-character HS256 secret is brute-forceable offline in seconds from any captured access token, after which an attacker forges tokens for arbitrary user ids - and because the same JWT_ACCESS_SECRET is deliberately shared by every service that verifies user tokens (.env.dev02.example:92-95), one weak value is total platform compromise, not one service's.

**Fix.** Change all three to z.string().min(32) (or at minimum .min(1) for parity), and apply the same floor to JWT_ADMIN_SECRET in backoffice-service.

### AIM-85 — INTERNAL_SHARED_SECRET is documented as guarding internal service routes but is never read by any code

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/community-service/src/config/env.ts:41`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/deploy/dev02/.env.dev02.example:89`
**Checklist:** P3.1 env config that misrepresents an implemented control — flagged by P3 Pre-deploy audit

```
/**
   * Shared secret for unauthenticated internal (service-to-service) routes such
   * as the gateway's public-card lookup for the link preview. When unset, the
   * internal routes are disabled (return 404) - they are never public.
   */
  INTERNAL_SHARED_SECRET: z.string().optional(),
```

**Impact.** A grep for INTERNAL_SHARED_SECRET across all nine services returns only this declaration and a comment; community-service has no middleware, route or handler that reads it. The gateway's card lookup was rewritten to call a plain unauthenticated route instead (apps/api-gateway/src/linkhost/public-card.ts:21-25 and 35-42). Meanwhile deploy/dev02/.env.dev02.example:88-89 tells the operator it "Guards the internal HTTP routes between api-gateway and community-service" and the website Dockerfile (lines 41-43) lists it as a required server-only secret. The risk is not a direct bypass - it is that operators and future reviewers believe an authentication layer is protecting the internal community routes when no such check exists, so the real protection (network isolation) is never verified and any future internal route added there inherits an imaginary guard.

**Fix.** Delete the dead variable from community-service's schema, the dev02 env template and the website Dockerfile comment - or implement the header check it claims to describe. Do not leave a security control documented but unimplemented.

### AIM-86 — Unauthenticated backoffice health endpoints leak environment name and live database/Redis reachability

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/backoffice-service/src/routes/health.routes.ts:16`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/backoffice-service/src/routes/health.routes.ts:44`, `aimess_backend/apps/backoffice-service/src/app.ts:58`
**Checklist:** P5.1 health/metrics endpoints leaking versions, env, DB state — flagged by P3 Pre-deploy audit, P5 Internal exposure

```
res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    service: SERVICE_SLUG,
    title: SERVICE_TITLE,
    environment: env.NODE_ENV,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  });
```

**Impact.** healthRouter is mounted at both /health and /v1/health before serviceRoutes and outside adminAuth (apps/backoffice-service/src/app.ts:58-59). HAProxy proxies all of backoffice.ai5dev.tech to :3010 with no path filter (deploy/haproxy/dev02.cfg:104-108), so GET https://backoffice.ai5dev.tech/health is public and discloses NODE_ENV, and GET /health/ready (line 22) discloses per-dependency booleans for admin_db Postgres and Redis. That is free reconnaissance: it confirms the admin service exists at that hostname, names it, and tells an attacker when its backing store is degraded - useful for timing an attack against a service that has no rate limiting. The gateway's own /health (apps/api-gateway/src/routes/health.routes.ts:5) is correctly minimal by comparison, leaking no version, uptime, memory or service list.

**Fix.** Return a bare 200 with no body (or {ok:true}) on the liveness path, and move /health/ready behind adminAuth or restrict it to the proxy's source address - HAProxy's own check at dev02.cfg:106 originates from 127.0.0.1 and can be allowlisted.

### AIM-87 — AsyncAPI docs page executes third-party JavaScript from unpkg at a floating major version

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/docs/asyncapi.ts:50`
**Checklist:** P3.2 debug/doc surface hardening — flagged by P3 Pre-deploy audit

```
<script src="https://unpkg.com/@asyncapi/react-component@${REACT_COMPONENT_VERSION}/browser/standalone/index.js"></script>   (REACT_COMPONENT_VERSION = "2", line 22)
```

**Impact.** The page is served from the API origin (https://api.ai5dev.tech/docs/socket) with no CSP (helmet CSP is off, see the separate finding) and no subresource-integrity attribute, pinned only to major version 2 - so whatever unpkg resolves 2.x.x to at request time runs in the API origin. A compromised or hijacked package release, or an unpkg CDN incident, executes attacker JS on an origin that carries the platform's API cookies and is trusted by operators who open the docs. Same for the stylesheet on line 42.

**Fix.** Pin the exact version and add an integrity= hash, or vendor the standalone bundle into the gateway's static assets so the docs page loads nothing off-origin.

### AIM-88 — Firebase web config hardcoded as a literal fallback in committed frontend source

**Where:** `aimess_website/src/services/firebase.ts:5`
**Also at:** `aimess_website/public/firebase-messaging-sw.js:5`, `aimess_website/.env:62`, `aimess_website/.env:59`
**Checklist:** P1.4 frontend exposure — NEXT_PUBLIC_* / secrets reachable in client bundles; P1.1 hardcoded API keys — flagged by P1 Secret leak

```
apiKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_API_KEY || "«redacted»",
    authDomain: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_AUTH_DOMAIN || "aimess-app.firebaseapp.com",
```

**Impact.** The real aimess-app project's browser API key, sender id and app id are hardcoded as `||` fallbacks here and again unconditionally in the committed service worker aimess_website/public/firebase-messaging-sw.js:5 (both files are tracked — confirmed via git ls-files). Firebase web API keys are public identifiers by design and are shipped in every client bundle regardless, so this is not a confidentiality breach; the concrete risks are that the key is unrestricted-by-default (abusable for quota consumption against enabled Firebase APIs, and usable to enumerate the project) and that a hardcoded fallback silently keeps a stale project alive when the env var is later repointed. NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY in aimess_website/.env:62 carries the same value and is the higher-cost exposure — Maps keys are billable.

**Fix.** Restrict the key in the Google Cloud console: HTTP-referrer restrictions to the production origins and an API allowlist limited to FCM (and Maps JS for the Maps key), plus a billing quota cap. Drop the `||` literal fallbacks in firebase.ts so a missing env var fails loudly instead of silently binding to a hardcoded project; keep the service-worker values in sync via the existing scripts/check-firebase-sw.mjs check.

### AIM-89 — QR device-link token - a bearer credential redeemable for a full session on an unauthenticated namespace - is written to logs verbatim

**Where:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/auth.ns.ts:103`
**Also at:** `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/auth.ns.ts:119`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/auth.ns.ts:103`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/auth.ns.ts:87`, `aimess_backend/apps/api-gateway/src/sockets/namespaces/auth.ns.ts:117`
**Checklist:** P2.1 logging of PII / credentials — flagged by P1 Secret leak, P2 Personal-data flow

```
logger.warn(`/auth subscribe failed for qr:${token}: ${String(err)}`);
```

**Impact.** The /auth namespace is deliberately unauthenticated ("Public `/auth` namespace for the QR-login (linked devices) flow - no JWT", auth.ns.ts:17-19): anyone may emit auth:qr:subscribe with a linkToken and join room qr:<linkToken>. auth-service publishes the approval envelope to that room containing accessToken, refreshToken, deviceId and userId (device-link.service.ts:330-337), and publishQrLinkSuccess additionally parks a one-shot copy in Redis for 120 s that the FIRST subscriber to call takeQrLinkResult collects and deletes (user-socket.ts:133-160). So the linkToken is the only thing standing between an attacker and a full session. Logging it verbatim puts that credential into the log pipeline: anyone with log-read access (aggregator, SRE, a leaked log file) who sees a token inside the 120 s window can subscribe first and take the session envelope before the legitimate browser does. logger.warn prints at every level including production `info`.

**Fix.** Log a truncated digest instead of the token - the same treatment rate-limit.ts:55 already applies to session tokens (`createHash("sha256").update(token).digest("hex").slice(0,32)`) and sendPush.ts:118 applies to FCM tokens. Apply it to all three sites in this file.

## Refuted claims

Raised by a domain auditor, then disproved by the adversarial reviewer. Listed so they are not re-reported later.

- **docker-compose publishes MongoDB with no authentication and Redis with no password to host interfaces** — `aimess_backend/docker-compose.yml:46`  
  Why not: REFUTED for production. The facts in the file are accurate (mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all with no --auth at docker-compose.yml:46, 27017 published at :49, redis with no requirepass publishing 6379), but this is the local-dev compose and it says so in the comment immediately above line 46 ('Local dev runs WITHOUT auth... Production uses a managed MongoDB'). The production deployment does not use it: deploy/dev01/compose.yml:69-96 runs mongod with --keyFile plus MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME/PASSWORD and binds ${LAN_IP}:27017, deploy/dev02/compose.yml:128 dials it with credentials and authSource=admin, and every dev02 service is on a compose bridge with only four loopback-bound HTTP ports. …
- **media-service defaults its CORS allowlist to "*"** — `aimess_backend/apps/media-service/src/config/env.ts:27`  
  Why not: REFUTED as exploitable. The default is real (config/env.ts:27, consumed at app.ts:17-24), but three controls stack against it. deploy/dev02/compose.yml:201-202 explicitly sets CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: ${PUBLIC_WEB_ORIGINS} for media-service with the comment 'CORS is enforced at the gateway; media-service is not publicly routed', so the default is never taken in the production deployment. The service publishes no host port in that compose file. And api-gateway/src/proxy/create-service-proxy.ts:51-56 deletes every access-control-* header off proxied responses, so even a wildcard from downstream cannot reach a browser. The claim itself concedes this is latent; with no path from the internet it is …
- **Livestream comment history is scoped only by ban, not by community membership** — `aimess_backend/apps/stream-service/src/services/livestream-comment.service.ts:611`  
  Why not: Code matches the description (getComments checks banRepo.isBanned at livestream-comment.service.ts:611 and isCommunityBanned at 615-619, and nothing else), but this is not a defect: it is exactly the sanctioned design. checkAccess explicitly documents 'Viewing is always allowed (ban check above is the only hard gate). Membership only controls commenting: non-members can watch silently.' at apps/stream-service/src/services/livestream.service.ts:2050-2052, and a non-member who passes that gate joins the /stream room and receives the same comment backlog through the gRPC stream:join / stream:load_more path, which the doc comment at livestream-comment.service.ts:596-602 says intentionally …
- **Lightbox header builds HTML by string concatenation with no escaping** — `aimess_website/src/component/chat/messages/chatMediaLightbox.ts:270`  
  Why not: Sink text confirmed at :264-273 (`bar.innerHTML = ...${header.title}...`, avatar `<img src="${header.avatarUrl}">` at :265), but it is unreachable, and the auditor concedes this. injectLightboxHeader only runs behind `if (extras?.header)` at chatMediaLightbox.ts:437. There are exactly two consumers of the hook in the whole frontend — ChatMediaGallery.tsx:84 (`const { open } = useChatMediaLightbox()`) and MessageUserInfoPanel.tsx:284/385 (`openLightbox(lightboxMedia, index)`) — and neither passes a 5th `extras` argument; useChatMediaLightbox.ts:16-30 merely forwards an always-undefined value. No attacker-controlled data reaches innerHTML today, so this is dormant code, not an exploitable …
- **Unbounded page size on the pins endpoints reaches Prisma `take` directly** — `aimess_backend/apps/chat-service/src/api/controllers/community-message.controller.ts:1157`  
  Why not: Code is as described — controller :1157 `const limit = Number(req.query.limit) || 20`, route community.routes.ts:190 registered with no validateQuery, value reaching `take: params.limit` at community-message-pin.repository.ts:169 — but the amplification is refuted by an existing control. findPinsByRoom filters `unpinnedAt: null` (repository.ts:163-166) and active pins per room are capped by env.PIN_LIMIT_PER_ROOM (config/env.ts:67, default 50) enforced on the pin path at community-message.service.ts:3079-3080, so ?limit=100000000 still returns at most ~50 rows on this exact endpoint. The read is also fully authorized first via assertCommunityReadAccess (community-pin.service.ts:386-393). …
- **validateQuery merges the unvalidated raw query back over the parsed result, defeating zod's strip-unknown** — `aimess_backend/packages/utils/src/validate.ts:99`  
  Why not: The code is exactly as quoted (validate.ts:99-104 spreads `...req.query` before `...parsed.data`), and the description of the consequence is accurate — undeclared keys pass through unvalidated. But there is no exploit path, and the claim concedes it: every service is on express ^5.2.1 with the default "simple" query parser (grep for `query parser` / `query-parser` across aimess_backend/apps returns zero overrides), so values are strings or arrays of strings and no object literal can reach a Mongo $match. This is an accurate hardening observation about a hypothetical future config change, not a present defect; real=false on exploitability, keep as low-priority cleanup.
- **media-service echoes any client-supplied http(s) string back as a download URL** — `aimess_backend/apps/media-service/src/services/media.service.ts:528`  
  Why not: Line 528 confirmed verbatim (the `/^https?:\/\//i.test(params.objectKey)` short-circuit in generateDownloadUrl, :519-544). But no trust boundary is crossed: this is a read-only endpoint that reflects the caller's own request value back to the same caller. Nothing is persisted, nothing is fanned out to other users, no ownership or membership data is disclosed, and the claim itself concedes there is no SSRF because the server never fetches the URL. The "laundering" framing does not add impact — a client already had that URL in hand to send it. The only case where a third party's client feeds an attacker string into this path is when the string was already stored on a message, which is finding …
- **Unmaintained direct frontend dependencies: html2canvas and redux-persist** — `aimess_website/package.json:44`  
  Why not: REFUTED as a security finding. The lines exist (package.json:44 "html2canvas": "^1.4.1", :58 "redux-persist": "^6.0.0", :39 "crypto-js": "^4.2.0"), but the auditor states outright that neither package has a known exploitable CVE at these versions, and the claimed defect is entirely prospective ('any future parser defect'). There is no vulnerability in the repo to verify — 'last published release' is an upstream registry claim I cannot confirm from this tree, and it would not constitute an exploitable defect if true. This is dependency-maintenance tracking, outside the security-relevant scope. The real risk it gestures at (auth tokens in localStorage) is already claim 11.
- **assetlinks.json delegates the production deep-link domain to the debug build variant** — `aimess_website/public/.well-known/assetlinks.json:18`  
  Why not: REFUTED. The file is confirmed as described — the second statement at :14-25 grants handle_all_urls to com.aifivetech.aimess.app.debug at line 18 — but the mitigating control is in the same object: sha256_cert_fingerprints at :20-22 are byte-identical to the release entry's at :8-10 (B2:D0:AA..., E5:BC:9F..., 5F:A1:B0...). Android App Links verification matches on package name AND signing certificate, so only a build signed with the genuine release keys satisfies this entry; an attacker cannot produce one, and an ordinary debug build (signed with a debug keystore) will not verify against it either. There is no exploitable path today. The auditor concedes this in the claim body. The residual …
